title: Can AI help me make a portfolio reel from years of client work?
summary: Build a focused portfolio reel from past work by choosing the role you want to show, finding relevant source shots, and making your contribution clear.
body_markdown:
## What you’ll take away


- Choose the intended work and audience before collecting shots.
- Show your own contribution clearly when projects involve a larger team.
- Retain source references so the reel can be updated for a different opportunity.


## Choose the reel's job before searching the archive


A cinematography reel, an editing reel, and a brand-film portfolio need different evidence. Define what you want the viewer to hire you for. This determines whether a beautiful isolated shot, a sequence transition, or a complete narrative passage is more useful.


In an illustrative editing portfolio, a striking aerial shot may have little to do with the editor's distinctive work. A short sequence that turns an interview answer into a clear story may demonstrate more. Do not let the easiest shots to find decide the professional identity of the reel.


## Select work you can appropriately show


Identify which projects and materials are available for portfolio use, including any restrictions on unpublished work or third-party assets. Use your established agreements and approvals. Do not assume possession of the source files means every clip belongs in a public reel.


Make your role clear. If you edited a film shot by another team, describe the editing contribution rather than implying you created every element. A concise project credit or accompanying description can prevent an attractive montage from overstating authorship.


## Search for the evidence your reel needs


In Wideframe, point a chat at the eligible project folders and describe the visible subjects or actions you want to review. The[visual-search recipe](https://try.wideframe.com/skills/find-clips-visual/) can help locate source candidates. Add the public recipe when you want to save the recurring search task.


For an editor's reel, also identify finished passages whose construction matters. Source search can find material, but it cannot by itself explain who made the creative decisions in a finished project. Keep project context and your contribution attached to the candidates.


## Build a progression rather than a greatest-hits pile


Group the selected work by the capability it demonstrates. You might move from clear dialogue storytelling to product detail, then to an energetic sequence. Choose an opening that establishes the kind of work you want, not merely the loudest image.


Avoid repeating similar shots once the point is made. A reel with fewer distinct examples can communicate more than a long sequence of interchangeable moments. Let the structure show range where range matters and focus where specialization is the goal.


## Decide when a longer passage is more persuasive


Some craft disappears when reduced to a second-long flash. An interview transition, a comic timing decision, or an elegant product explanation may need a short uninterrupted passage. Give the viewer enough time to perceive the work.


For those examples, consider whether the reel should point to a fuller case study or project page. The reel can introduce the capability while the longer work demonstrates it. Do not force every project into the same shot length simply to maintain a montage rhythm.


## Finish the source-based reel for its destination


Prepare an editable sequence and refine it in Premiere. Keep titles and credits readable, choose sound that supports the presentation, and make the ending identify how to find more work. Use assets appropriate to the portfolio's intended distribution.


Retain the source relationships and alternate selections. When a client asks for a reel focused on a different kind of work, you can revise the argument rather than hunt through exports again. A source-based project is particularly useful when an older project needs to be removed or replaced.


## Update the reel when your goal changes


Do not add every new project automatically. Replace material when it better demonstrates the intended capability or reflects the work you now want. Keep a small set of useful candidates organized by role and type of contribution.


Return to Wideframe when a new opportunity calls for a different selection from the archive. The recurring job is finding evidence for a specific portfolio brief; the editorial judgment is deciding what that evidence says about your work.


## Try this request


TRY AN EXAMPLE REQUEST


Search these portfolio-eligible project folders for shots and passages that demonstrate \[specific capability\]. Keep source and project references, suggest distinct options rather than near-duplicates, and retain my supplied role notes with each candidate.
